context.problemStatement:
Implement the `Lambda` case of `eval`. An anonymous function `fn(x) { ... }`
evaluates to a function value. Nothing in its body is evaluated until it is
called, so this case never returns an error. Build a `VFunc(UserFn(...))` whose
name is `"lambda"` (used in error messages) and whose parent is the environment
in which this function was *defined*, not the one in which it will be called. This
is what lets a function use the names around it, even after the call that created it
has returned.

```
// In eval:
    Lambda(params, body) ->
      // YOUR CODE HERE (replace the code below)
      Error(errors.NotImplemented(
        "Lambda("
        <> string.inspect(params)
        <> ", "
        <> string.inspect(body)
        <> ")",
      ))
```

Run the tests:

```
gleam test -- q8
```

targets.claim: Student can explain why their Lambda case never returns an error even when the body of the anonymous function uses an unbound name, and when such an error would appear instead.

probes.question: In your `Lambda(params, body)` case, why does defining a function whose `body` contains an unbound variable not return an `Error`, and when would that unbound variable error actually be raised?
probes.reason: Directly assesses both why `Lambda` evaluation succeeds unconditionally and the exact phase when body evaluation and errors occur.

probes.question: If we evaluate `Lambda(["x"], Var("undefined_name"))`, what does your `eval` return immediately, and what needs to happen to trigger an error from `undefined_name`?
probes.reason: Grounds the explanation in a concrete expression to test whether the student understands that lambda creation defers body evaluation until invocation.

content: In your `Lambda(params, body)` case, why does defining a function whose `body` contains an unbound variable not return an `Error`, and when would that unbound variable error actually be raised?
it would only return an error when eval is called on Lambda

reason: The student claimed an error occurs when eval is called on Lambda, which is factually incorrect since eval on Lambda immediately returns Ok(VFunc(...)) without evaluating the body.

content: Not quite. Look at your `Lambda(params, body)` case in `eval`—what does it return when `eval` is called on a `Lambda`, and when does its `body` actually get evaluated?
It returns a function value, so it wouldnt return an error until that function is evaluated

reason: The student correctly identified that defining a lambda simply returns a function value without evaluating the body, and the error only arises later when that function itself is called/evaluated.
